title: Lowest Cap for K Spaced Picks
statement:
You get an array nums and an integer k. You must pick at least k positions, and no two picked positions may be next to each other.

The cap of a choice is the largest value among the picked positions. Return the smallest cap any valid choice can have. It is guaranteed that k spaced positions exist.

examples.why: Pick positions 1 and 3 (values 1 and 2). They are not neighbours, and the larger value is 2.
The two smallest values, 1 and 2, sit next to each other. The best spaced pair is 4 and 2, with cap 4.
The only three spaced positions are 0, 2 and 4.

hints: Flip the question: for a given cap c, can you pick k spaced positions whose values are all at most c?
That yes/no check is greedy. Walk left to right and take every allowed position as soon as you can, then skip its neighbour. Taking early never blocks more than waiting would.
The check is monotone in c: a larger cap only allows more positions. Binary search the smallest c that passes.

explain.intuition:
Minimising a maximum is a strong hint for binary search on the answer. Fix a cap c. Now every position is simply allowed (value ≤ c) or not, and the question becomes: how many non-adjacent allowed positions can you take? Scan left to right and take an allowed position whenever the previous one was not taken. Taking the earliest possible position is safe, because it can only block the very next position, which a later choice would block just as well.

If cap c works, any bigger cap works too, since it allows a superset of positions. So binary search over the values between min(nums) and max(nums) for the first cap where the greedy count reaches k.
steps: Write enough(c): walk the array; when nums[i] ≤ c, count it and skip index i + 1. Return whether the count reaches k.
While lo < hi: if enough(mid), set hi = mid, else lo = mid + 1.
pitfalls: Taking the k smallest values. They may be neighbours, as in [4, 1, 2, 7, 9].
Running a full max-sum DP inside the check. You only need the count of picks, and the greedy count is optimal for that.
Searching for exactly k picks. At least k is the requirement, and the greedy may find more, which is fine.

complexity.time: O(n log M), M = largest value

solutions.title: Try every value as the cap
solutions.idea: Sort the distinct values and run the greedy check for each, from smallest up. The first one that passes is the answer.

solutions.title: Binary search on the cap with a greedy check
solutions.idea: Binary search the smallest cap for which picking allowed positions greedily from the left yields at least k.

followups: Search over the sorted distinct values instead of the numeric range. When does that help?
The positions form a ring, so the first and last are neighbours. What changes in the check?
